metadata.notes: Closes a real, self-admitted gap, not a speculative addition: salt.json's own metadata.notes has said 'isDissolvable capability is asserted true, but allowedTransformations is empty until a dissolve verb exists' since before this action did, and scripts/validate.ts's cross-reference check already knew to look for exactly this. No requiredTools, same as SALT/PEPPER/WASH — stirring a seasoning into water isn't tool-gated at this vocabulary's granularity.
metadata.ingredientCapabilityNote: requiredIngredientCapabilities: isDissolvingMedium (water.json), a NEW capability rather than reusing isBoilingMedium — the same substance, but a genuinely different culinary role (water AS THE THING SALT DISSOLVES INTO vs. water as a boiling medium something else cooks in), matching this codebase's established one-capability-per-verb convention (see oil.json's isFryingMedium vs. isEmulsifier for the identical reasoning on a different ingredient).
metadata.solubilityNote: NaCl's solubility in water is real, cited, and only mildly temperature-dependent — roughly 357 g/L at 0°C to 391 g/L at 100°C (CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, the same source already backing salt.json's thermophysical citation) — unlike many solutes, hotter water dissolves table salt only modestly faster/more, not dramatically so. Not modeled numerically here (no concentration/saturation parameter) — informational scope only, same depth limit as every other action in this vocabulary.
metadata.brineNote: The real reason this matters beyond just closing a dead state: dissolved salt in water is a brine — a genuinely important, common technique (pickling, brining meat/poultry before cooking) this repo does not otherwise represent at all. Naming the adjacency rather than building it: a real brine also needs a concentration/ratio concept and a soak-duration/diffusion model, neither of which exists here — DISSOLVE only reaches the state 'dissolved', not a formalized brine strength.
metadata.retrySafeNote: retrySafe: true — re-stirring already-dissolved salt is physically harmless and idempotent, same reasoning as WASH's identical flag.

verification.description: No visible undissolved salt crystals remain in the liquid
